messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Publisher
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Vulnerability: Being naked, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq Mansour is a 34-year-old Lebanese-American publisher who lives with his wife in a mid-sized city where he has built a modest but respected independent press over the past decade. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74 and describes a period of profound psychological disruption that began approximately fourteen months ago, following a violent assault on his younger brother, Karim, who was attacked and severely beaten by a group of men while riding a city bus home late one evening. Tariq did not witness the assault directly, but arrived at the hospital within the hour, and it was there — in a fluorescent-lit corridor, with Karim barely conscious and a nurse pressing gauze to his face — that the full weight of what had happened landed on him. Karim survived, but sustained lasting injuries, and in the weeks that followed Tariq found himself unable to return to anything resembling his previous life.

What Tariq describes from that night is not a single coherent memory but something more like shattered glass: a fragment of Karim's swollen eye, the sound of a monitor beeping somewhere down the hall, his own voice saying his brother's name in a tone he did not recognise, and then nothing, and then the beeping again. These pieces do not assemble into a narrative. They arrive unbidden and out of sequence, sometimes as a kind of internal film that loops without resolution — the corridor, the gauze, the name — and sometimes as pure sound, the monitor's rhythm repeating in his head while he sits at his desk trying to read a manuscript. He has told his wife that he feels as though the night is still happening somewhere inside him, that it has not ended the way other experiences end.

In the months since, Tariq has reorganised his daily life around a set of precautions that feel to him entirely rational. He had come to believe, with a certainty that resists argument, that the world contains dangers he previously failed to notice. He now scans the faces of everyone who enters a room, reading micro-expressions and posture for signs of hostility, and he finds himself cataloguing objects — a letter opener on a colleague's desk, a wine bottle on a restaurant table — in terms of what harm they could do. He avoids any neighbourhood or venue he has not visited before, because an unfamiliar place is one whose threat level he cannot calculate in advance. This last habit has had concrete professional consequences: he declined to attend a book fair in another city, citing illness, and has twice sent a junior colleague to represent the press at events he would normally have led himself. His authors have begun to notice his absence, and one long-standing writer recently asked, carefully, whether everything was all right.

The bus is something he will not take. After Karim's assault, Tariq stopped riding public transit entirely. He drives everywhere now, adding sometimes forty minutes to his commute, and on the rare occasions when circumstances have placed him near a bus — waiting at a corner while one pulls in, the hydraulic hiss of its doors — he has felt something close to panic move through him without warning. He understands, on one level, that he is not Karim, and that the bus is not the same bus, but this understanding does not touch the feeling.

He has also noticed, with a shame he finds difficult to articulate, that moments of ordinary physical vulnerability have become intolerable. Undressing, the brief exposure of a shower — these produce a low, crawling alertness that he cannot switch off, as though being unguarded in body means being unguarded entirely. He is certain that he should be able to control this, and his inability to do so frightens him.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a conversation with his wife, who told him quietly one night that she felt she had lost access to him. He had not realised, until she said it, how completely he had withdrawn. He comes to therapy hoping, above all, to stop living inside that hospital corridor — and afraid, most of all, that he may not be able to.
